idiom_name: module-level dict[str, Callable] filled by an @register decorator
implementation_notes: The kit is a module-level dict from key to callable plus a decorator that performs the registration: @register('csv') sits on the class or the factory function, and create(key, *args) looks the callable up and raises an error naming the available keys when it is missing. functools.partial pre-binds constructor arguments the registering module chose, which is the 'builder captures its dependencies' step; no class hierarchy survives the translation, because Python's first-class functions make the product's construction an ordinary callable. Keep the dict private to the module, expose unregister/reset for tests, and remember that decorator registration only runs when the defining module is imported - a silently missing key is the standard failure. Prefer this variant for in-tree implementations; use the entry-points variant when implementations come from installed distributions.
pitfalls: A module-level dict lives as long as the interpreter, so registrations leak between tests; expose reset/unregister and use it in fixtures, or make the kit an instance with its own table.
Registration happens on import: a lazily imported module or a misspelled entry point yields an unknown-key error at create time instead of a startup failure.

Storing classes and calling cls(*args) assumes compatible constructor signatures; store a callable (functools.partial for fixed arguments) so each product's constructor stays the registering module's business.

variants.name: Packaged plugin discovery via importlib.metadata entry points
variants.implementation_notes: The same table is filled from packaging metadata instead of from imports: each installed distribution advertises its factories under a group (pyproject.toml [project.entry-points."myapp.shapes"]), and the host asks for entry_points(group=...), resolving each match with load(), which imports the target lazily - so a plugin's code is only loaded when its key is requested. The selectable entry_points(group=...) API is available from Python 3.10; earlier versions returned a mapping keyed by group. Choose it when the set of implementations is decided by installation rather than by the application, guard every load() so one broken distribution cannot sink discovery, and keep an explicit in-process registry for first-party types where determinism and testability matter more.
pitfalls: Discovery scans the installed distributions, so start-up cost and results depend on the environment; two distributions can advertise the same name and silently collide unless you check.
entry_points(group=...) is Python 3.10+; older interpreters need the importlib_metadata backport or the deprecated dict form keyed by group.
ep.load() imports code chosen by whatever is installed, so never run discovery in an environment whose distributions are not trusted.
